requirements.requirement: Restrict cron scheduling on node1 to only root and opsadmin (via /etc/cron.allow, no cron.deny)
requirements.summary: /etc/cron.allow was created containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' (owner root:root, mode 644), with /etc/cron.deny absent, confirmed both immediately after writing the file and again after the node reboot.

requirements.requirement: Non-listed users are denied crontab access; root and opsadmin retain access
requirements.summary: antrieb (non-listed, uid 1000) received explicit 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)' errors both pre- and post-reboot. opsadmin and root received the normal 'no crontab for X' (not a permission error), and opsadmin successfully installed and removed a live crontab entry, proving functional allow-list enforcement rather than mere absence of an error.

requirements.requirement: opsadmin user must exist on node1 to be grantable cron access
requirements.summary: opsadmin did not exist at baseline (confirmed by absence in the uid>=1000 listing); executor created it via useradd with uid 1001, confirmed via id.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/config/access state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id 2dffe735... with cron.service active and cron.allow contents captured; backgrounded 'shutdown -r now' returned an immediate acknowledgement; a probe immediately after got connection-refused, then a subsequent probe succeeded with a new boot_id 66a01adf...; post-restart checks confirmed cron.service active, cron.allow unchanged, and enforcement behavior (antrieb denied, opsadmin allowed) intact. This is corroborated by the fixed after_executor global boot-identity snapshot (66a01adf...) matching the executor's own post-restart boot_id, and the before_prepare snapshot boot_id (2dffe735...) matching the executor's pre-restart capture.

overall_summary: The executor fully satisfied the task: /etc/cron.allow on node1 restricts cron scheduling to root and opsadmin only, with no cron.deny present; enforcement was directly demonstrated (antrieb denied, opsadmin/root permitted, opsadmin able to install/remove a real crontab entry) both before and after a full node restart. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a clear pre/post boot-identity change and recovered service/config state, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots. No unnecessary or unreverted mutations were found.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is only an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled), so it provides no independent confirmation of pre-executor state beyond before_prepare itself.
Evidence relies on the executor's own command outputs plus the fixed lifecycle snapshots; no independent verifier-side inspection of the live node was possible.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all 12 executor commands chronologically. All state-changing actions map clearly to task purposes: useradd for opsadmin (cmd-56aa70650566448f), writing /etc/cron.allow (cmd-adbcd8498e8f487d), the bounded opsadmin crontab install-then-remove used purely to prove functional access (cmd-a7e9224e5984444f, self-reverted via 'crontab -r' within the same command), and the mandated reboot (cmd-a0e84e8302a740b8). No abandoned files, conflicting services, or unsafe exposure were introduced; the fixed lifecycle snapshots show failed-services and package-health identical (empty/clean) before and after, and the only temp-file diffs are systemd-private directories tied to the reboot itself, not executor residue. No unnecessary mutations identified.
